full_judgment: 13. Mr. Fazlul Karim, learned, advocate for the appellant, argued before us that the statements of the deceased were arbitrarily discarded on the ground that they were not corroborated by independent witnesses and circumstances and probabilities. Upon examining the evidence on record it seems there were other substantial grounds to doubt the alleged statements of the deceased. As far as Ext. 2 the alleged dying declaration recorded by the doctor is concerned the same clearly deserves to be ignored because admittedly it was not a voluntary statement of the deceased but was made in response to questions put by the doctor and the questions were not admittedly recorded by the doctor. The Additional Sessions Judge has noticed if those questions were leading questions Ext. 2 could not be accepted as genuine. Secondly the High Court Division noticed that there was interpolation in the statement by different pen. On top of all this there was a big question as to whether the deceased was physically in a position to make such lengthy statements at Islampur Thana Dispensary where his condition was found to be grave. P.W. 13, the doctor who examined him at about 9 p.m.(Exts. 2 and 3 were allegedly recorded at the same time, 9 p.m.) stated that all the injuries (15) were profusely bleeding and fresh. Condition of the injured was very grave and O.C Islampur P.S. was duly informed. It is difficult to understand how the doctor and the Police-Officer could record such lengthy statements at the same time. The O.C. said in his evidence that he learned from the doctor that the condition of Shamser Ali Amin was bad and that he might sink at any time. It is again beyond comprehension as to how such a sinking man was made to give such long statement in great details. We have seen Ext. 3. (Ext. 2) has not been brought on the paper book by the appellant) and it is a matter for great puzzle to see that the sinking man could make a statement with such completeness as would put a man in his full sense to shame. In the circumstances it is difficult to brush aside the defence suggestion that Exts. 2 and 3 were not the words of the deceased but were subsequently created for the purpose of the case. The prosecution case in so far as it was sought to be based on the alleged statement of the deceased was, therefore, not free from doubt and in the circumstances one can find not much fault if a court disbelieves the rest of the evidence on the basis of some reasonable grounds. Having considered the matter as a whole we are satisfied that there has been no miscarriage of justice on account of the order of acquittal and therefore no interference is called for with the impugned order of the High Court Division.
